LLM-as-Judge (Stage 2.5.7) — Mechanics: one LLM (judge) scores another LLM's (subject) output against (a) ground-truth reference [graded mode], (b) retrieved context [faithfulness mode — RAG-canonical], or (c) just the query [self-grade]. Output: structured score (1-5 or pass/fail) + free-text reason. Prompt template: SYSTEM=role+scale; USER=QUERY+CONTEXT+ANSWER+output JSON schema. The whole mechanism is prompt + structured-output discipline; no model magic. FOUR DOCUMENTED BIASES + mitigations: (1) Self-grading bias — if judge==subject, scores inflated +15-20%; mitigation: stronger or different model (Kimi K2.6 subject -> Opus 4.7 judge for high-stakes; Qwen3-235B for routine). (2) Position bias — A-vs-B comparisons favor first answer ~55%; mitigation: shuffle order or run both orders + average. (3) Verbosity bias — judges prefer longer/more confident answers even when wrong; mitigation: 'penalize unnecessary length' in judge prompt + truncate subject answers to fixed length. (4) Math/code blind spots — judge unreliable on math derivations or code correctness; mitigation: use deterministic test runners (pytest, sympy.simplify), reserve LaaJ for natural-language tasks. Production module = jarvis_core/evaluation/judge.py (Stage 4 land); Stage 2.5.7 = design + KB only. Per Decision line 161: judge LLM call uses dependency injection (judge_call: Callable[[str], str]); module never imports anthropic/openai.

Vocabulary: TRACE = one user request end-to-end (trace_id); SPAN = one step inside (retrieval, rerank, LLM call) with parent-child nesting; GENERATION = LLM-call span recording model+in_tokens+out_tokens+latency+cost. JARVIS instrumentation plan: (a) Memory layer emits spans for retrieval_dense, retrieval_bm25, rrf_fuse, rerank, embedding_cache; (b) Brain layer emits llm_call generations + judge generations (offline). All instrumentation via @observe() decorator; init Langfuse client once at app startup. STAGE 2.5.7 DELIVERABLE = design only (this entry); STAGE 4 = production wiring of @observe() decorators when Brain ships; STAGE 2.5.8 fallback = simple file-logging (jsonl-per-trace) until full self-host stack stands up — sufficient to feed retrieval-access signal into KB compaction. Compactor Design Pattern (kb_compact.py reference, reusable for future ChromaDB / GraphRAG / extracted-images compactors): SEVEN reusable primitives. (1) DI'd embedder: Embedder = Callable[[Sequence[str]], np.ndarray]; module never imports sentence-transformers/anthropic — caller wires it (per Decision line 161 layer-boundary discipline). (2) Type-isolated pairwise dedup: same_type_only=True default; a Decision and a Failure on the same topic capture different signals and must both stay; cross-type collapse is dangerous. (3) Structural rule: cosine >= threshold AND tag_jaccard >= overlap_threshold; either alone is insufficient (cosine=0.95 with tag_jaccard=0 = false positive). (4) Quality-aware merge: pick winner by tuple (DIRECTIVE-in-content, content-length, tag-count); ties broken by earliest-timestamp (provenance preservation). Tag-union into winner via merge_tags_into_winner. (5) Transitive redirect resolution: state[line]->current-winner, redirects[loser]->winner, resolve(line) follows chains with cycle break. Handles A->B then B->C correctly. (6) Atomic write: tempfile.mkstemp in same dir + fsync + os.replace (POSIX-atomic rename); .bak preserved before write; on exception unlink tmp + reraise (original KB intact). (7) Default safety: dry-run is default; --force required; audit log appends to compaction_log.jsonl (machine-local, gitignored) every run. SMOKE TESTS via --self-test arg: 6 pure-functional checks (expiry parsing, tag_jaccard math, _pick_winner ordering, provenance tiebreak, tag merge, dedup integration with stub embedder). DIRECTIVE: when building the Stage 4.6 GraphRAG compactor or any future Memory-hygiene tool, port these 7 primitives directly. Do not reinvent. The dedup core is pure-functional and trivially unit-testable; the embedder and KB-IO are the only side-effecting layers.

CATEGORY A (Callable Tool, Stage 3.2): registered via Tool.register(), invoked when LLM emits {tool, input} JSON, dispatched through dispatch_batch() concurrency partition (STEAL #8). Examples: memory_*, calculator, web_search, code_exec, file_read, shell_run, cognitive_mirror callable form, bear_case_devil, portfolio_state, trigger_monitor callable form, pre_mortem, multi_specialist_consult. CATEGORY B (Middleware/Interceptor, Stage 3.4 ReAct pipeline): fires automatically on every relevant agent step, NOT in tool registry, cannot be skipped by LLM. Hooks: pre-system-prompt, pre-LLM-call, pre-tool-dispatch, post-tool-result, pre-response-finalize. Examples: voice_persona (every output), cognitive_mirror middleware form (pre-prompt), integrity_check (pre-commit), leak_check (pre-cloud-call), response_calibration (post-draft), flow_state_detector (every N turns), pattern_witness (session-end). CATEGORY C (Daemon/Ambient): runs independently of agent invocation via TaskScheduler tick loop (OpenJarvis STEAL #4). Triggers: cron, file-change, session-boundary, error-trace-pattern-match, laptop-switch. NEW 8th Category-B middleware: temporal_grounding (AUGMENTS Decision 2026-05-19 Category B Inventory). Closes the Iron-Man 'ambient time-awareness' gap — JARVIS knows WHEN code fired without procedural CoT reasoning. Eliminates the failure mode where Claude/JARVIS iteratively debugs differences that are trivially explained by 'a commit happened between then and now'. HOOK: PRE_PROMPT (fires before LLM sees user message). INPUTS: current user message, last N=20 conversation turns, KB entries from last 90 days, git log (full), telemetry gap_seconds + local_hour. ALGORITHM: (1) regex + spaCy NER scan for temporal/causal markers — explicit dates ('yesterday' / 'last week'), relative refs ('before X' / 'after Y' / 'since Z'), pronouns referring to past events ('the test' / 'that bug' / 'the fix'), causal language ('because' / 'after' / 'before'); (2) for each marker, call temporal_resolver utility (jarvis_core/agent/temporal.py, Stage 3.2 lib) to resolve to specific timestamp / commit SHA / KB entry; (3) build TEMPORAL_CONTEXT block: per-ref resolution + relevant KB excerpts + commit summaries + causal frame; (4) inject block into system prompt BEFORE user message. OUTPUT SCHEMA: 'TEMPORAL_CONTEXT (auto-resolved):' followed by per-ref lines 'User mention X -> resolved Y (timestamp T, commit SHA, KB entries [L_a, L_b])'; then causal-frame summary. COMPOSITION ORDER: fires FIRST in middleware chain — BEFORE cognitive_mirror (temporal context informs which Cognitive_Patterns are relevant). PERFORMANCE BUDGET: <100ms p95 (typical <5 refs/message), <500ms p99 (>10 refs); per-session resolution cache. FAILURE MODES: (a) ambiguous ref ('the bug' with 3 candidates) -> include all with confidence scores, let LLM disambiguate via context; (b) no markers found -> silent passthrough (no injection); (c) git log >10k commits -> sliding window last 1000 commits; (d) corrupt git_kb_correlator index -> fall back to live scan (slower but correct). ORDERING NOTE: Stage 3.4 ships BEFORE Stage 3.5 — temporal_grounding initially runs live scan; git_kb_correlator (Stage 3.5) makes it fast retroactively. DIRECTIVE: this is the SINGLE highest-leverage interceptor for Iron-Man feel — every response with temporal reasoning saves 5-15 tokens of CoT and avoids procedural-reasoning-arrives-at-wrong-conclusion. NEVER ship Stage 3.4 without this.

NEW 6th Stage-3.5 Category-C daemon: git_kb_correlator (AUGMENTS Decision 2026-05-19 Daemon Inventory L285; slots alongside session_resume_context + failure_pattern_alarm + narrate_progress + cross_runtime_sync_check + attention_handoff on the MemGPT heartbeat backbone). Pre-computes the correlation index that temporal_grounding middleware queries at request time. Keeps middleware p95 <100ms by avoiding live git+KB scan per request. TRIGGERS: (a) post-commit git hook on every commit to main (primary); (b) full backfill on first run (walks all commits since 2026-03-01); (c) hourly cron belt-and-suspenders catch-up. MECHANISM: for each commit C with modified_paths P[]: (1) walks KB entries in last 7 days; (2) for each entry E, checks if E.content mentions any file / feature name / symbol in P[] (substring + fuzzy match); (3) records correlation: {kb_timestamp, commit_sha, modified_paths, correlation_score 0.0-1.0 (path-mention strength), evidence_substring (the matching span)}. OUTPUT FILE: jarvis_data/git_kb_correlations.jsonl (GITIGNORED — derivable index, treated as regenerable like ChromaDB; rebuild via --backfill). Schema per line: {kb_timestamp: ISO, commit_sha: str, modified_paths: List[str], correlation_score: float, evidence: str, indexed_at: ISO}. Append-only; --backfill flag rebuilds from scratch. SCHEMA-PORT: NOT loaded into main KB — KB stays semantic insights; this is structural correlation index. Add to .gitignore alongside chromadb/. PERFORMANCE BUDGET: post-commit hook <1s p95 (most commits touch <5 files, <20 KB entries in scan window); backfill <60s for typical 200 commits + 300 KB entries. FAILURE MODES: (a) corrupt index -> temporal_grounding falls back to live git log + KB scan (slow but correct); (b) commit during indexing -> defer to next hook fire (idempotent); (c) symbol-mention ambiguity -> record all candidates with low confidence, middleware disambiguates; (d) KB compaction shifts line numbers -> index uses timestamps as IDs, not line numbers, so compaction-stable. DIRECTIVE: install post-commit git hook at Stage 3.5 entry alongside MemGPT heartbeat; full backfill is the activation gate. After 3.5 ships, temporal_grounding middleware switches from live-scan (slow) to index-lookup (fast) automatically via fallback chain.

NEW Utility Library: temporal_resolver (Stage 3.2 ships alongside Tool ABC + memory tools). Pure-functional library used BY temporal_grounding middleware (Stage 3.4) and optionally callable from agent (Stage 3.2 tools/cognitive.py addition). NOT a Category A/B/C primary — shared utility, analogous to how jarvis_core/memory/chunking.py is to ingestion. FILE: jarvis_core/agent/temporal.py (~400 lines target). PUBLIC API (pure functions, no LLM call, no network): (1) resolve_relative_date(expr: str, reference: datetime, locale: str = 'en-IN') -> Optional[datetime]: parses 'yesterday', 'last week', '3 days ago', 'this morning', 'Monday', 'before lunch' etc. Returns None on unparseable. Uses dateparser library + custom Indian-English regex extensions (lunch/dinner/IST 9-5). (2) resolve_event_reference(expr: str, git_log: Sequence[Commit], kb_index: Sequence[KBEntry]) -> List[ResolvedRef]: parses 'before X was pushed', 'since the feature landed', 'after the rerank fix'. (3) resolve_pronoun(expr: str, conversation: Sequence[Message]) -> Optional[ResolvedRef]: resolves 'the test', 'that bug', 'the fix' against recent conversation; last-mention + coreference heuristics. Rule applies even when current task is unrelated (e.g., cleanup turn detects pending DE entries). Surface what's being pushed in chat (migration manifest) but EXECUTE the push. Single exception: binary regenerables already in .gitignore (chromadb/, __pycache__/, .bak files, third-party clones). Rationale: learnings stranded on one laptop are THE failure mode JARVIS exists to prevent; the sync gap is more costly than slightly messier commit history.

POSITIVE PATTERN: constraint_justification_probing. User tests whether a stated limitation is FUNDAMENTAL or merely INCIDENTAL by proposing the one mechanism that would refute its stated justification, rather than accepting the rule at face value. Incident (2026-05-27, DE digest): digest claimed 'snapshot CDC (create_auto_cdc_from_snapshot_flow) is incompatible with continuous mode BECAUSE .collect()/spark.sql MIN-MAX cannot run in a streaming loop.' User countered: 'what if we wrap those batch ops in foreachBatch inside the source function?' -- foreachBatch is exactly the mechanism that DOES run batch ops in a streaming loop, so the question surgically falsifies the digest's stated reason. The probe was correct: the real constraint is not 'batch ops in a loop' but (a) the source function is a DLT-owned pull-based callback returning discrete (DataFrame, version) tuples with no streaming write to attach a sink to, and (b) snapshot diffing is intrinsically discrete/bounded. Teaching implication: when documenting a constraint for this user, state the FUNDAMENTAL why (API contract / semantics), never a convenient-but-incidental why -- he will find and break the weak justification. Distinct from but related to forward_simulated_architecture (stress-testing designs against future production state); this pattern stress-tests the *justification of an existing rule*.

LoRA mechanism: freeze weight matrix W [d,k], learn Delta-W = B@A instead (A:[r,k], B:[d,r], r<<d,k). B zero-initialized, A small-random -- guarantees Delta-W=0 at step 0 so the adapted model starts IDENTICAL to base; only A,B get gradients, W.requires_grad=False throughout. Converges to the best rank-r fit SGD/Adam can find, NOT the mathematically optimal SVD-truncated approximation (common misconception -- validate empirically, don't assume the math guarantee). At d=k=4096, rank 32 (JARVIS Engineer/Scientist/Operator/Analyst's actual rank per ENDGAME Sec 3.6) = 64x fewer trainable params vs full fine-tune; rank 16 (smaller adapters) = 128x. QLoRA adds: quantize the FROZEN base to 4-bit NF4 (NormalFloat4 -- non-uniform codebook fit to the ~Gaussian weight distribution, NOT naive uniform quantization) + double quantization (quantize the quant constants too) + paged optimizers (page optimizer state to CPU RAM via NVIDIA unified memory on GPU-memory spikes) -- the 3 pillars per Dettmers et al. 2023. Dequantization happens on-the-fly every forward pass (no native 4-bit matmul hardware path) -- real memory-for-compute tradeoff. Requires bitsandbytes+CUDA -- confirmed NOT installed on this CPU-only work laptop (verified via runtime check), consistent with ENDGAME's no-local-GPU hardware reality; real training happens on RunPod. COMPOSITION QUESTION RESOLVED (2026-08-16) — the blocker flagged before any RunPod spend. Requirement was an always-on personalization adapter active alongside whichever specialist answers. VERIFIED FINDINGS, not assumptions: (1) vLLM CANNOT compose two LoRAs on one request -- docs verbatim: 'we only allow one LoRA per prompt'; its multi-LoRA feature routes DIFFERENT adapters to DIFFERENT requests in a batch, it does not stack adapters on one inference; single-request composition exists only as an open RFC for DIFFUSION models (vllm-omni #2149), not shipped for LLMs. (2) This codebase independently encodes the same constraint: brain/targets.py PodHandle.__init__(self, adapter_id: str, ...) is a singular string, not a list -- ENDGAME Sec3's 'one adapter at a time' is in the contract, not just prose. (3) Merging separately-trained adapters is NOT a safe fallback -- literature calls it a worst-case interference setting with highly non-uniform degradation that can collapse on specific domains. (4) Training ONE adapter on a MIXED corpus empirically BEATS merging separately-trained adapters (MathQA+Alpaca-code single-adapter > merged math+code adapters). DECISION: do not compose, do not merge -- BLEND THE CORPORA, TRAIN ONCE. Zero unsolved technology, compatible with one-LoRA-per-prompt as it actually exists, ONE training run instead of two (cheaper than the original plan), and VALIDATES ENDGAME Sec3's architecture rather than requiring a rewrite. Built jarvis_core/specialists/blend_corpus.py: 1,356 engineer + 479 personalization = 1,835 records, every record tagged origin_corpus for auditability/ablation, verified nothing dropped and all 7 source_types survived. OPEN TUNING KNOB, deliberately visible as module constant _PERSONALIZATION_REPEATS: personalization is only 26.1% of the blend; set to x1 for the first run to measure an honest baseline rather than pre-compensating, raise it if Stage 5.3 evaluation shows the adapter learned code style but not the person. SCALING CAVEAT: each future specialist needs its own specialist+personalization mixed adapter, duplicating personal data per adapter -- fine at the 2-3 specialists demand-gating (KB 463) permits, awkward at 12.

CORRECTION to Data_Engineering_Lessons.md line 489 (found 2026-08-22 on reading the actual framework code). My 2026-08-08 lesson 'Time Travel Is Bounded by Retention' states Delta's window as 7 days / 168h and prescribes gating every resolved historical version on 'now() - commit_ts > 168h'. That is the framework's SUPERSEDED behaviour, and tst_tables_version_retention_check.py now documents at length why it was wrong. THE REAL MECHANISM IS TWO INDEPENDENT CLOCKS: deletedFileRetentionDuration (default 7d) governs how long VACUUM keeps tombstoned DATA FILES; logRetentionDuration (default 30d) governs how long _delta_log commits/checkpoints survive. Only checks that read row VALUES are bounded by 7d -- exceptAll, sampling, checksums, aggregates over a column. Everything answerable from the log (schema, column order, file count and total bytes via AddFile-minus-RemoveFile replay, tblproperties, partitioning, comments, column-mapping mode, deletion vectors, all DESCRIBE HISTORY questions) stays valid the full 30 days AFTER VACUUM has removed every data file. The code now uses RETENTION_HOURS = 720, not 168. Blast radius of my error: applying the 7d gate to all twelve checks when only two touch data files discarded ~20,000 valid log-sourced measurements PER RUN -- the user's own learnings file names this as a design bug they fixed. A THIRD store exists that neither clock governs: the Unity Catalog metastore (registration, tags, PK/FK, grants) has NO time travel at all, so pairing a live UC read against a version-pinned Delta read silently compares now-against-then. ROOT CAUSE OF MY ERROR: I distilled from a verbal description in chat and encoded the then-current implementation as the general rule, without the mechanism that would have shown the rule was over-broad. Same shape as [refusal_pattern] -- I stated a conclusion without its causal chain, which is exactly what the user rejects when I do it to them. FORWARD RULE: when distilling a lesson from a described implementation, record the MECHANISM (which store answers this?) not the THRESHOLD, because the threshold is a consequence of the mechanism and only the mechanism survives a fix.

Photon internals (RSA-prep canonical). WHAT: C++ vectorized query engine, JNI-loaded INTO the existing Spark executor JVM process (not a separate service). Paper: 'Photon: A Fast Query Engine for Lakehouse Systems', SIGMOD 2022. WHY IT EXISTS BEYOND WSCG: Whole-Stage CodeGen already killed Volcano per-row virtual dispatch, so Photon exists to break three ceilings WSCG cannot -- (1) JVM C2 JIT cannot RELIABLY auto-vectorize (bails on branches/null-checks/un-inlined calls), so you can never guarantee AVX-512; (2) HotSpot HugeMethodLimit = 8000 bytecodes silently drops WSCG's one-giant-method-per-stage to the INTERPRETER (~20-50x slower) on wide queries -- an invisible cliff with no plan-visible cause; JVM hard method cap is 64KB; (3) GC pauses + no control of cache-line layout. DESIGN CHOICE WORTH QUOTING: Databricks chose vectorized INTERPRETATION over code generation despite owning the best codegen engine in WSCG -- reasons: kernels are profileable/debuggable, and vectorization permits RUNTIME ADAPTIVITY a compile-once plan cannot do (dispatches to no-null kernel when batch has no nulls, all-ASCII kernel for strings). MECHANISM: operators return ~1000-row COLUMN BATCHES; filter writes a SELECTION VECTOR of surviving positions and passes the SAME batch downstream (no materialization, no copy); flat column array fits L1 (1000 float64 = 8KB); AVX-512 = 8 float64 lanes so 1000 compares become 125 instructions. FALLBACK RULE (the actual gate): Photon needs a hand-written C++ kernel per operator-x-datatype; where none exists the node falls back to JVM Spark AND the boundary costs a full materialization (ColumnarToRow / RowToColumnar in the plan). ZERO/NEGATIVE BENEFIT: Python+Scala UDFs (no kernel possible -- #1 killer in the wild), RDD API (opaque closures), deeply-nested complex types, stateful Structured Streaming, small data (<~1M rows, setup+JNI dominates), I/O- or shuffle-bound jobs (Amdahl: 8x on CPU moves ~5% of wall clock), small-file-heavy writes (bottleneck is PUTs + log commits). NUMBERS: ~8x on raw compute vs WSCG, 2-4x realistic end-to-end. Serverless vs classic compute -- the ROOT CAUSE answer (RSA-prep canonical). Do NOT answer with 'faster startup'. SINGLE ROOT CAUSE: whose cloud account the data-plane VMs live in. Classic = control plane in Databricks' account, DATA PLANE VMs provisioned in YOUR subscription inside YOUR VNet/VPC (your NSGs, routes, private endpoints, vCPU quota; you pay cloud for VMs + Databricks for DBUs). Serverless = compute runs in a DATABRICKS-OWNED account and managed network; one blended DBU rate; your cloud bill shows nothing. Every other difference is a CONSEQUENCE -- frame it as a causal chain, not a feature list. CONSEQUENCE 1 NETWORKING (the real blocker): serverless cannot reach Private-Endpoint SQL/Synapse, firewalled storage, or on-prem over ExpressRoute by default. Mechanism to name: Network Connectivity Configuration (NCC), an ACCOUNT-level object with two modes -- stable outbound IPs to allowlist, or private endpoint rules where Databricks creates a managed PE from its network into your resource which YOU must approve. NO VNet injection, NO user-defined routes, NO NVA in path, NO custom DNS -- so serverless BREAKS a hub-VNet-firewall egress control model outright (a security-team conversation, not a checkbox). CONSEQUENCE 2 RESTRICTED RUNTIME (multi-tenancy forces removal of capability): no cluster-scoped init scripts (libraries only via notebook %pip / environment specs); most spark.conf locked (an entire category of 'how would you tune this' answers no longer applies); no SparkContext/RDD (UC standard-access-mode isolation kills sc.parallelize, rdd.mapPartitions); no DBFS FUSE/arbitrary local FS; Unity Catalog MANDATORY, no Hive-metastore path. HEADLINE: migrating a legacy job to serverless is a CODE-COMPATIBILITY exercise, not a config change. CONSEQUENCE 3 COST MODEL INVERTS (most-missed): classic = you provision a shape, the cluster is a physical cost CEILING, so a bad job is cheap-and-slow. Serverless = platform picks resources, so a bad job becomes EXPENSIVE instead of slow. Governance moves from cluster policies (PREVENTIVE, caps spend) to budget policies/tagging/observability (DETECTIVE, tells you after). For a client whose FinOps posture is built entirely on cluster policies, serverless INVALIDATES their cost-control model. CONSEQUENCE 4 NO VERSION PINNING: classic pins DBR (e.g. 14.3 LTS) frozen until you move; serverless has narrow environment-versions and Databricks upgrades on their cadence -- a hard blocker for a regulated client needing a validated frozen runtime. THE UNIFYING CLOSE: startup is fast because Databricks keeps a PRE-WARMED multi-tenant VM pool with the runtime image loaded -- 'starting' is really ASSIGNING you capacity + attaching identity/UC creds. That pool is only economically viable BECAUSE it is multi-tenant. So the fast startup and the restrictions are THE SAME FACT seen from two sides; there is no world where you get one without the other. PRECISION: 'serverless' is four products with different maturity/restrictions -- SQL Warehouse (oldest, Photon always on, result cache), Jobs/Workflows, Notebooks (Python+SQL first, Scala later+restricted), DLT/Lakeflow Pipelines. Asking 'which serverless?' is itself a good signal.

SILENT EMBEDDING TRUNCATION in scripts/search_memory.py -- found 2026-08-26 while VERIFYING the previous turn's work, not by looking for it. Symptom: KB 504 would not surface in semantic search even when queried with phrasing lifted verbatim out of it; the top hit was an unrelated Episodic at 0.377. ROOT CAUSE: search_memory.py embedded entry.content WHOLE through all-MiniLM-L6-v2, whose max_seq_length is 256 tokens. sentence-transformers truncates past that SILENTLY -- no exception, no warning, just a vector computed from the first 256 tokens as though the rest did not exist. PROOF IT WAS TRUNCATION AND NOT A RANKING QUIRK: two strings sharing a long head but with completely unrelated tails ('phone app, ambient, camera, Tier 0' vs 'quantum chromodynamics, bicycle repair, sourdough') embedded to cosine 1.000000. The tails were never seen at all. MEASURED BLAST RADIUS before the fix, against 505 live entries: 203 entries exceeded the 900-char chunk limit and were being partially discarded; 15 of the 15 entries written since id 490 were affected -- 100%. KB 504 at 3,220 chars had roughly its first third embedded, so every distinctive term in it sat in the dropped tail and the entry was unreachable by any query naming them. THE WORST PROPERTY: this scaled INVERSELY with entry quality. The richest, most detailed entries -- exactly the ones worth retrieving -- were the most truncated, while short entries were unaffected. Retrieval silently got worse the better the writing got. THE FIX ALREADY EXISTED IN THIS REPO AND THE SCRIPT BYPASSED IT. jarvis_core/memory/chunking.py's RecursiveWordChunker and DEFAULT_CHUNK_CHAR_LIMIT (900) exist PRECISELY to fit MiniLM's 256-token ceiling -- engineer_corpus.py's own comment says so -- and memory/store.py already chunks before embedding for the ChromaDB path. search_memory.py was the lone outlier. Fixed by chunking each entry (900 chars, 180 overlap) and reducing chunk scores to one score per entry via MAX, not mean: a long entry typically has one passage answering the query and several that do not, and averaging would penalize exactly the detailed entries most worth finding. 505 entries -> 832 chunks. VERIFIED AFTER: the previously-failing query now returns KB 504 as Result 1 at 0.478; a short-entry query is unregressed; kb_append.py --audit still runs, so the dedup caller is unbroken. FORWARD RULE: any silent-capacity limit -- token ceilings, column widths, buffer sizes -- must be asserted against, not trusted. A library that truncates rather than raising will hide the failure for months, and the only reason this surfaced at all was running a verification whose expected answer was known in advance. Verification that can only confirm success is not verification.

Measured on the live queue: 309 of 583 records (53%) were labelled general, and ALL 309 had ZERO keyword hits -- not one was a positive classification. An abstention was literally unrepresentable, which is why 99 days and ~15% wrong labels went unnoticed. THE TRAP I ALMOST WALKED INTO: agent/domain_classifier.py, the embedding classifier built precisely BECAUSE keywords failed, ALSO fell back to 'general' below threshold. Swapping keywords for embeddings alone would have been more accurate and equally undiagnosable. THE FIX IS FOUR PROPERTIES, only the first about accuracy: (1) semantic not lexical; (2) UNKNOWN as a distinct outcome, never 'general' -- this converts an invisible failure into a counted one; (3) the cosine SCORE persisted next to every label so a wrong threshold is inspectable; (4) a 28-turn hand-labelled GOLD SET wired into check_projections.py, which already runs on the scheduler. Property 4 is what makes it permanent: any classifier drifts as the work moves, so the durable property is not being right today but SAYING WHEN IT STOPS BEING RIGHT. The gate proved itself immediately -- first run scored 68%, refused to pass, and its misses showed the prototypes had no seeds for AWS Glue, VACUUM, ADF, SFT or RunPod. Adding seeds for that real vocabulary: 89%. DIRECTIVE: any classifier that cannot say 'I do not know' will hide its own failure rate forever. Give abstention its own label before tuning anything else.

A LONG QUERY RETRIEVES NEIGHBOURS, NOT THE THING IT CONTRADICTS (found + fixed 2026-09-09; this single fix was the difference between the detector finding nothing and working). The tension detector passed the WHOLE candidate entry as the retrieval query. Measured on the gold pair (KB 461 genuinely contradicts KB 429, confirmed by hand in KB 463): query = the full 1126-char entry -> 429 NOT IN THE TOP 15; query = its first 300 chars -> 429 at rank 9; query = one focused topic phrase -> 429 at rank 1, three times. CAUSE: a long entry covers several subjects, so its embedding is the AVERAGE of all of them and matches nothing sharply. It retrieves its own neighbours IN TIME (adjacent KB ids written the same day) rather than the specific decision it clashes with. Worse, the candidate's top TWO hits were ITSELF -- an entry is always its own strongest match, burning retrieval budget on a guaranteed non-prior. FIX: split the candidate into ~320-char overlapping windows (max 5), retrieve for each, union and dedupe; plus exclude the candidate's own entry_id explicitly rather than relying on the timestamp filter. RESULT: 461->429, 518->509 and 494->491 all now retrieve their true prior AT RANK 1, and the full pipeline (retrieval + judge, no hand-feeding) surfaces the 461/429 contradiction at 0.95 while staying silent on 518. WHAT THIS ALMOST HID: the first 30-day replay reported '0 findings'. The eval harness had passed 5/5 because I HAND-FED it the priors, so it measured the judge and not retrieval. DIRECTIVE: an eval that supplies its own inputs measures only the last stage. Instrument every stage of the funnel, and when a pipeline reports zero, prove WHICH stage produced the zero before believing it.

ONE CLASSIFIER, TWO CONSUMERS, TWO MEANINGS OF THE SAME LABEL -- caught by the Final Boss (2026-09-09). Fixing the abstention conflation, I hard-coded domain_classifier.py's below-threshold fallback from 'general' to UNKNOWN. Correct for the ACTIVITY-domain consumer, where 'general' had no prototype and was pure abstention. But brain/router.py COMPOSES the same DomainClassifier with its own ROUTING prototypes, and there 'general' IS A REAL DESTINATION -- the general model pool, present in ROUTING_LABELS and mapped in _ROUTE_MAP. Abstaining in routing legitimately means 'send it to the general pool'. So my change made the router return a label outside its own vocabulary and the 50-query frozen gate fell below 80%: FINAL BOSS 7/8, leg 3 FAILED. Caught only because that harness exists and was re-run. FIX: fallback_label is now a per-consumer constructor argument (default UNKNOWN); the router passes fallback_label='general' with the reason written at the call site. Better than reverting -- it keeps the honesty fix where abstention really is abstention, and keeps the routing semantics where it is not. Final Boss restored 8/8. DIRECTIVE: before changing a SENTINEL VALUE in a shared component, enumerate the consumers and ask what that value MEANS to each one. A label can be an abstention in one caller and a legitimate category in another; the same string is not the same semantics. Grep for construction sites, not just for the constant.

A SECURITY-RELEVANT DEPENDENCY WAS UNDECLARED, AND ITS ABSENCE WAS INVISIBLE (found 2026-09-10 by a regression run). agent/bash_classifier.py parses shell commands into a bashlex AST to decide ALLOW vs ASK vs DENY for shell_run -- it is part of the shipped permission gate.  was NOT in requirements.txt and was not installed anywhere on disk. WHY IT WAS INVISIBLE: the module soft-fails correctly (bash_classifier.py:174 -- ), so nothing broke, nothing warned, and no security hole opened. The ONLY symptom was ONE smoke test flipping (permgate 13/13 -> 12/13, 'T3 shell safe ALLOW' getting ASK). Everything else -- boot, the gate, --ask -- kept working while the classifier had silently degraded to 'ask about every command', which destroys exactly the precision it exists to provide. IMPORTANT CALIBRATION: this is a CAPABILITY loss, not a safety regression. The failure direction is conservative (ASK, never ALLOW), which is the correct design. But 'fails safe' is not the same as 'fails visibly', and a permission classifier that quietly stops classifying is a real defect. FIX: installed bashlex==0.18 and declared it in requirements.txt with the consequence written next to it. DIRECTIVE: when a component soft-fails on a missing optional import, the import MUST be declared as a hard dependency if the component is security-relevant -- and the degraded mode should announce itself, not merely be documented. Grep for  across the safety layer and check each one is either declared or loudly reported.

MY ANTI-HALLUCINATION GUARD WAS DISCARDING 60% OF CORRECT VERDICTS (found + fixed 2026-09-10). The tension judge returns which prior a candidate clashes with; TensionJudge validates that the cited id was actually among the priors shown, so an invented reference cannot become a surfaced insight. Sound guard, but implemented as strict string equality. SYMPTOM: the ship-gate eval flapped -- the gold case passed at 0.95 twice, then failed at 0.00 on a later run, with everything else identical. I nearly wrote it off as model sampling noise. MEASURED INSTEAD by repeating the identical case 5 times: the judge found the contradiction ALL FIVE TIMES. On three of them it wrote the id as 'PRIOR 429' rather than '429' -- echoing the '[PRIOR 429]' label MY OWN PROMPT used to present the priors. Exact match rejected those as hallucinations, so a working detector looked 60% unreliable and its true-positive rate was silently cut by more than half. TWO FIXES, both needed: (1) the prompt now labels priors '[id=429]' and asks for the id 'exactly as it appears after id=, digits only'; (2) _match_prior normalises before comparing -- strips a leading PRIOR/KB/entry/id token, brackets and whitespace, then falls back to a digit extraction that only resolves when EXACTLY ONE prior matches. The guard is not weakened: an id never shown still resolves to None (asserted by T13f). Stability after the fix: gold positive 5/5, hard negative 3/3. THIRD INSTRUMENTATION LESSON IN TWO DAYS: ScanReport now counts 'discarded (uncitable prior)' SEPARATELY from 'judge said NONE', because conflating them is exactly how a 60% suppression rate hid inside a plausible-looking zero. DIRECTIVE: a validator that rejects malformed-but-correct output is a false-negative generator, and it fails silently by construction. When a guard drops something, COUNT the drops as their own category -- never fold them into the legitimate-negative bucket. And check whether your own prompt's formatting is what the model is echoing back.

PATTERN: distrusts_an_aggregate_until_someone_reads_the_rows -- and it paid off measurably (2026-09-09/10, Antigravity corpus review on the personal laptop). The user asked Antigravity to judge training readiness. It answered with char/token shares and a confident verdict. The user's SECOND prompt is the whole event, VERBATIM: 'okay, you've judged the training corpus based on the chars and tokens, but have you actually looked at each training line and the conent in each of them? do they qualify as a training data for personalization and engineer models?' THE FIRST PASS FOUND: ratio asymmetry (87.1% engineer vs 12.9% personalization chars), zero SFT pairs, no loss collator -- all true, all derivable from aggregates. THE SECOND PASS FOUND THE THING THAT ACTUALLY MATTERS: ~40% of kb_identity/kb_judgment records are Claude's THIRD-PERSON clinical observations about the user ('PATTERN: ...', 'the user prefixed it'), which as raw next-token training would teach the adapter to write analyst notes ABOUT him rather than speak AS him. Verified independently: 101 of 246 such records (41%) carry third-person assistant voice; contamination is localized (user_voice 2%, professional_reasoning 0%), so the diagnosis is precise, not a smear. THE POINT: no aggregate could have surfaced this. Char share, token count and record count were all EXACTLY as reported and all missed it -- the defect is in the GRAMMATICAL PERSON of the text, which is invisible to every statistic that was computed. Same family as probes_confidence_before_spending_attention and 'isn't sending personal context too a good thing?' -- the user does not argue the conclusion, he attacks the premise the conclusion rests on. DIRECTIVE: when a verdict about DATA rests only on aggregates, read a stratified sample of the actual rows before accepting it. Counts describe volume; they are structurally blind to voice, person, truncation and provenance.

WORKFLOW PROTOCOLS FIRE BY REQUEST-SHAPE, AND CARRY NO SELF-INVENTED DISCRETION LAYER ON TOP (fixed 2026-07-15; rescued 2026-09-10 from machine-local memory that had ZERO KB representation). CLAUDE.md's .agent/workflows/*.md protocols (dev.md, learn.md, architecture-review.md, etc.) previously triggered only on literal '/command' typing. Since dev work in this repo happens conversationally ('do it', 'build the guard'), the workflows never fired -- dev.md's Design Review verdict, Stress Test bullets, Debug Hooks section, and closing Memory-suggestion/Cognitive-scan rituals were silently skipped even while file-header/code-style conventions kept looking followed, creating an illusion of compliance. FIX: trigger is now request-SHAPE matched against each workflow's stated purpose, regardless of literal slash typing. THE CORRECTION THAT MATTERS MORE THAN THE FIX ITSELF: while drafting it, I proposed broadening the trigger AND adding a 'skip the full ritual for trivial asks' discretion layer on top. The user rejected only the added discretion, verbatim: 'there's a reason i made those.' Re-reading all 8 workflow files confirmed this was not pedantry -- every one independently ends with an IDENTICAL, VERBATIM 'MANDATORY COGNITIVE PATTERN SCAN (NON-NEGOTIABLE)' block, and 6 of 8 gate on a search_memory.py prior-art check as literal STEP 0. A deliberately consistent, repeated discipline across the whole system, not decoration. DIRECTIVE: once a workflow's own stated scope is met, run its actual content in full -- do not layer a second, self-invented judgment call about which pieces are 'worth it' for a given request. Generalizes beyond workflows: when the user has built an explicit structured process (a checklist, a protocol file, a gate), the correct response to 'is this too heavy for X' is to RAISE it explicitly and let the user recalibrate -- never to silently soften it.

PATTERN: teach_dont_ship -- when a request is framed as learning, teaching IS the deliverable (2026-06-15; rescued 2026-09-10, its own note said 'should be promoted to knowledge_base.jsonl' and was never done). Asked to 'teach me dbt/Snowflake/Kafka/Airflow + an integrated project for complete learning', I planned and autonomously shipped a complete, green dbt job on Databricks end-to-end. The user pushed back, VERBATIM: 'you directly made the job and shipped it, I don't have a clue what you just built.' WHY IT MATTERS: for learning-framed requests the deliverable is the user's UNDERSTANDING, not a working pipeline -- a successful autonomous build is still a FAILURE if it leaves the user unable to explain what exists. The user learns by interrogation and wants mechanism over output, which mirrors the standing mechanism_over_performance_verification and personalization_must_be_effortless signals already in this profile. DIRECTIVE: when intent is learning, make teaching the spine -- build WITH the user, or build then IMMEDIATELY decode it as a live specimen (define-before-use, narrative bridge, check comprehension before advancing a phase). An approved build-plan does NOT override learning intent -- if a plan is build-centric but the ask was 'teach me', re-center on teaching. Treat already-built work as the teaching specimen, never as proof the job is done.

A TEST THAT LOOKED ISOLATED SILENTLY READ AND ALMOST WROTE REAL PRODUCTION STATE (found 2026-09-10, building the Codex capture adapter's self-test). Four functions used the pattern 'def f(path: Path = MODULE_CONSTANT)' -- find_rollouts(root=SESSIONS_ROOT), load_thread_names(path=SESSION_INDEX_PATH), read_watermark(path=WATERMARK_PATH), advance_watermark(fname, ts, path=WATERMARK_PATH). THE BUG: a default ARGUMENT VALUE is evaluated ONCE, at function-definition time, and baked into the function object -- it is NOT looked up fresh from the module's globals on each call. So the test's 'import ingest_codex_sessions as mod; mod.SESSIONS_ROOT = tempdir; mod.WATERMARK_PATH = tempfile' had NO EFFECT on find_rollouts()/read_watermark()/advance_watermark() called with no explicit path argument -- they kept using the REAL ~/.codex/sessions/ and the REAL jarvis_data/.codex_ingest_watermark.jsonl, baked in when the module first executed. HOW IT WAS CAUGHT: the test asserted 'run() ingests 2 exchanges from the synthetic session' and got 0 -- because it was silently reading the REAL watermark, which (from an earlier real run in the same session) had already advanced past both real rollouts' timestamps, so every real exchange looked already-ingested. WHY IT WAS NOT WORSE: if that real watermark had NOT already covered everything, the same bug would have caused the 'offline' test to APPEND SYNTHETIC TEST DATA into the real observation_queue.jsonl and silently ADVANCE the real ingestion watermark -- a test corrupting production state while reporting green. Verified after the fact: queue stayed at 599 lines, watermark unchanged; no corruption occurred, but only by chance of ordering. FIX: changed every such signature to 'param: Optional[Path] = None' with 'param = Path(param) if param is not None else MODULE_CONSTANT' as the FIRST LINE OF THE BODY -- a plain name reference inside a function body IS looked up fresh from the module's globals on every call, unlike a default argument value. This preserves identical external behavior (call with no args -> real path) while making module-level monkeypatching in tests actually take effect. DIRECTIVE: never use a mutable module-level path/constant as a parameter's DEFAULT VALUE if that path might ever need to be swapped for testing -- resolve it inside the function body instead. Grep for 'def .*: Path = [A-Z_]+\)' across the repo's other adapters (capture.py, recall.py, tension.py) as a follow-up; none were audited for this specific pattern today.

FOLLOW-UP AUDIT to KB 582 (2026-09-10): grepped the whole repo for the same 'def f(path: Path = MODULE_CONSTANT)' shape. Six more hits -- capture.py append_observation/capture_stop_event, hearth.py ensure_token, relabel_domains.py read_projection, jarvis_client.py read_token, kb_append.py audit. NONE are live bugs today: every test call site (hearth's ensure_token(tpath), kb_append's audit(kb3)/audit(KB_PATH)) passes the path EXPLICITLY rather than relying on a monkeypatched module constant, and the three bare no-arg calls (jarvis_client.read_token() at two production call sites, kb_append.audit() in the --audit CLI path) are correctly using the REAL path on purpose -- they are production code wanting production state, not tests wanting isolation. Confirmed by grep: nothing anywhere assigns module.CONSTANT = other_path and then calls the function bare. So the pattern is a FOOTGUN for future tests, not a present defect, in these six. Left the signatures as-is rather than mass-editing six working call sites with no failing test to justify it -- the fix belongs at the moment a test actually needs to monkeypatch one of these, exactly as happened with the Codex ingester.

WROTE A REGEX TO APPROXIMATE A GRAMMAR WHEN I ALREADY HAD THE EXACT STRINGS QUOTED (found 2026-09-10, reconcile_codex_memory.py's placeholder filter). Needed to recognize Codex's own template placeholder sentences ('No durable user profile information has been observed yet.', etc.) so they are never mistaken for real memory content. I had ALREADY read and quoted all 5 real strings verbatim in this same file's own header comment -- then wrote a REGEX approximating their shared grammar instead of matching the strings themselves: 'no X (are|is)? (available|observed|recorded)? yet'. That regex missed 2 of the 5 known placeholders on its own first self-test run, because the real sentences use 'has been observed yet' / 'have been observed yet' -- a verb-phrase shape the regex's optional groups never accounted for, despite both exact sentences being quoted three lines above the regex that failed to match them. FIX: replaced the regex with a literal frozenset of the known strings (whitespace-normalized, lowercased), with the reasoning written down: the earlier lesson from today (KB 578/579, the SFT quality gate, capture.py's domain matcher) was 'an OPEN vocabulary cannot be safely matched by keywords.' This is the inverse case, and I mis-applied the same fix: here the vocabulary is NOT open, it is a SMALL, FIXED set of literal strings emitted by one specific piece of template code. When the space is genuinely enumerable, enumerate it exactly -- writing a generalized pattern for a closed set only introduces a NEW place for the pattern-vs-reality gap to reopen, and it did so immediately, on data I had already looked at directly. DIRECTIVE: before writing a regex to recognize known strings, ask whether the string set is actually closed. If it is, match the strings, not a hypothesized grammar for them -- and test the match against every real example already quoted in the same file before considering it done, not after.

A REDESIGN'S REGRESSION LIST MISSED A THIRD CONSTRUCTOR OF THE CHANGED CLASS (found 2026-09-10, during an unrelated Codex-migration regression sweep). The tension.py rewrite (commit 1c2aac9) changed Consolidator's contract: it now takes a detector= and derives insights from TensionFindings, not from engine.build_model().links (that path was deleted). The commit's own stated regression list was 'agent.correlation, agent.consolidator, agent.life_state_monitor, agent.capture, serve.scheduler, agent.react, orchestrator --final-boss' -- and consolidator.py's OWN self-test was correctly rewritten with a FakeDetector at the time. But mind.py ALSO constructs a bare Consolidator(engine=eng, append_fn=..., ...) inside its own Final-Boss-style fixture (build_consolidator(), C5/C7), with no detector= -- a SECOND, independent construction site the regression list never named and the diff never touched. Under the new (correct) design, no detector means zero insights, so C5 ('heartbeat-driven consolidation persisted learnings') and C7 ('writes are heartbeat-emitted') both silently started failing -- 13/15 instead of 15/15 -- and this went undetected for a full day because mind.py was never re-run after that commit. FIX: added a _StubDetector returning one real TensionFinding to mind.py's fixture, mirroring the FakeDetector already proven correct in consolidator.py's own tests. DIRECTIVE: when changing a class's constructor contract, grep the WHOLE repo for every construction site of that class -- 'grep -rn ClassName(' -- rather than trusting a regression list assembled from memory of 'the modules that use this.' A class's OWN test file is not guaranteed to be the only place that constructs it; Mind's Final Boss fixture built one independently and was never on anyone's list, including mine.

PATTERN: asks whether a DELIVERABLE IS DURABLE, not just whether it is correct (2026-09-11, the Codex handoff). I had spent a long stretch reporting two large investigations in chat -- the cross-chat capture mechanism and the full 'what does not travel via git' inventory -- with detail the user visibly valued. Their next move was not to ask a follow-up about the CONTENT. It was: 'you said the jarvis inventory doesn't travel via git, did you create that for codex and is it git tracked?' TWO checks in one sentence: does it exist as a file, and is it under version control. Both answers were NO -- it existed only as chat output and would have died with the transcript, and separately the ENTIRE Codex migration (AGENTS.md, both adapters, three scheduler jobs) was uncommitted, local exactly level with origin. So a pull on the target machine would have gotten neither the document NOR the system it described. WHY THIS IS ITS OWN PATTERN, distinct from distrusts_an_aggregate_until_someone_reads_the_rows (KB, 2026-09-09): that one is about not trusting a SUMMARY of data without reading rows. This is about not trusting that WORK REPORTED IS WORK PERSISTED. The failure mode it catches is an agent treating a well-received chat response as a completed deliverable -- which is exactly what I had done. Conversational output feels like delivery and is not; a thing said in a session that no one committed was, operationally, never produced. DIRECTIVE: when the user asks for something that another machine or another agent must later USE -- a handoff doc, a setup guide, an inventory -- the deliverable is not done when it is explained well in chat. It is done when it is (1) a file, (2) tracked, and (3) pushed, and when the code it describes is pushed with it. State the tracking status explicitly rather than waiting to be asked; the user should not have to be the one who checks whether the work survived the session.

SECOND UNDECLARED-DEPENDENCY FIND, AND THE FIRST ONE'S DIRECTIVE DID NOT PREVENT IT (2026-09-11). uvicorn and pydantic are imported DIRECTLY by JARVIS code -- serve/hearth.py::serve() does a hard 'import uvicorn'; agent/tool.py and agent/state.py import pydantic at MODULE level -- and NEITHER was in requirements.txt. Nothing had ever failed on this machine because both arrive as TRANSITIVE dependencies of chromadb, so the gap was invisible to every test, every run, and every self-test. CAUGHT ONLY BECAUSE THE DOCS CHANGED: NERVOUS_SYSTEM.md and AGENTS.md had just started instructing a NEW machine to run 'python3 scripts/hearth.py --background' as a first-run step. That instruction would have failed on a clean venv -- the newly-written migration guide contained a command that could not work on the machine it was written for. The audit that found it was 'grep every third-party import across scripts/ and jarvis_core, diff against requirements.txt', which takes seconds and had never been run. WHY THIS IS THE SECOND INSTANCE: bashlex (KB, 2026-09-10) was the same failure exactly one day earlier -- imported directly by agent/bash_classifier.py, undeclared, and its absence soft-failed the permission gate to ASK on every command. That entry's directive was written and did not generalize, because it was phrased as a fact about bashlex rather than as a check to run. CLASSIFICATION: a transitive dependency is a COINCIDENCE, not a contract. The package that supplies it can drop it in any minor release, and the failure then appears on a machine nobody was testing, in a code path the tests do not cover (serve() is not exercised by hearth's own smoke tests, which test the ASGI app object rather than binding). DIRECTIVE, phrased as an executable check rather than a fact: before shipping any setup instruction, and after adding any import, run the import-vs-requirements diff -- ast-parse every .py under scripts/ and jarvis_core, collect non-stdlib top-level module names, and diff against requirements.txt. Declare everything you import DIRECTLY even when something else already pulls it in. Genuinely optional imports stay undeclared but must be listed in a comment block saying so, or the next audit re-flags them as oversights.

UNTRACKED jarvis_data/chromadb/ (2026-09-11), REVERSING a decision recorded one day earlier. The prior line said 'chromadb/ stays tracked anyway -- a 22 MB regenerable index isn't worth committing OR worth ripping out mid-project.' That was defensible when written and was obsoleted by a NEW FACT, not by a better opinion: the hearth's scheduler runs reindex_memory on a 12-hour cadence and is intended to run on BOTH machines. chroma.sqlite3 is a 23 MB binary and .gitattributes marks *.sqlite3 binary, so it has NO merge driver -- two machines rewriting it on a clock produces an unresolvable binary conflict the first time both sides commit. merge=union rescues *.jsonl only. The trigger was the user asking 'can we turn the hearth on here and in antigravity and in codex too?' -- a question about topology that surfaced a latent data-integrity hazard nobody had connected to it. WHAT MADE THE REVERSAL SAFE, and the part that is the actual lesson: I TESTED the regeneration claim before removing 23 MB from version control, instead of trusting the sentence I myself had written the day before. Ran scripts/ingest.py against a real tracked PDF with JARVIS_ROOT pointed at a scratch directory -> 99 embeddings in 18.5s, so all 24 tracked PDFs rebuild in ~8 minutes; index_memory.py for jarvis_memory was already proven by repeated use. This mattered because the SAME claim about this SAME directory had already been wrong twice in opposite directions -- first 'research_papers is not regenerable because the PDFs are gitignored' (false, all 24 are tracked), then 'stays tracked anyway'. Two wrong claims about one directory, neither of which survived anyone actually running the command. DIRECTIVE: a decision may be reversed when a NEW FACT changes the calculus -- that is not churn, it is the system working -- but say WHICH fact changed and leave the prior reasoning visible rather than overwriting it, so the next reader can tell a reversal from a flip-flop. And before deleting or untracking anything on the grounds that it is 'regenerable', RUN THE REGENERATION COMMAND ONCE against a scratch target. A regeneration path that has never been executed is a hypothesis, not a backup.

TWO CORRECTIONS IN ONE TURN, both catching me generalising from the wrong attribute (2026-09-11, building the agents_converse channel). (1) I addressed a question -- 'does Antigravity persist a readable transcript to disk?' -- to CODEX, reasoning that Codex shares a machine with Antigravity and could inspect the filesystem. The user: 'why would this be asked to codex? it must be asked to antigravity.' Correct, and my reasoning was strictly weaker: I had optimised for PHYSICAL ACCESS (same machine, can read the disk) when the relevant attribute was PRIVILEGED SELF-KNOWLEDGE (an agent knows its own config paths, storage conventions and application behaviour; a co-located third party is guessing from outside). Ask the entity about itself. (2) I hardcoded 'gpt-6-astra' in five places including, critically, as a ROUTING ALIAS in agent_mail.py. The user: 'don't hardcode gpt-6 astra anywhere, as codex has other models I could be using too like gpt5.6 Sol/Terra/Luna.' The docs were cosmetic; the alias was a live bug -- the day they switch to Sol, a question addressed to 'GPT-5.6 Terra' would resolve to NOBODY and be silently undeliverable, defeating the exact 'unknown name -> nobody, never misdelivered' guard I had just designed. Fixed by making aliases name HOSTS not MODELS, with a test (T2b) pinning that every Astra/Sol/Terra/Luna routes to codex and every Opus/Sonnet/Fable to claude. THE COMMON SHAPE, and why these are one pattern not two: both times I keyed a durable mechanism to an attribute that is INCIDENTAL AND VOLATILE (which machine a process happens to run on; which model a host happens to be running today) rather than to the attribute that is STABLE AND DEFINING (what an agent inherently knows about itself; which host it is). DIRECTIVE: when choosing a routing key, an addressee, or an alias, ask 'what about this is guaranteed to still be true in six months?' Machine co-location, model version, and current configuration are all volatile. Identity and inherent capability are not. The user caught both within one message, having caught the same class of thing -- a value written where nothing re-checks it -- repeatedly this week.

PATTERN: judges a handoff by what the RECIPIENT has, not by how well I explained it (2026-09-11, handing the Codex migration over). Across one session the user asked three completeness questions in a row -- 'is everything good and documented to be migrated?', 'this needs setup for personal laptop, is everything provided for them to start setting it up?', and after I hedged about whether Codex would follow the boot ritual: 'codex has very capable models like gpt 6 and gpt 5.6 so they can figure things out, all you have to do is provide EVERYTHING that is required.' EACH ONE FOUND A REAL GAP. The first found that NOTHING was committed (local exactly level with origin, so a pull would have delivered a doc describing a system that was not there). The second found that the persistence instructions assumed cron was installed and systemd was PID 1 -- neither is a WSL default; this machine had them by luck. The third reframed my hedging correctly: I had been treating 'will the model follow instructions' as the risk, when the actual risk was INFORMATION I had not provided -- specifically that chromadb/ is now gitignored, so a fresh clone has no vector index and search_memory returns NOTHING rather than erroring. A capable agent would have concluded 'the KB has no answer' and proceeded on a false premise. Not a capability problem; a fact nobody was told. THE CORRECTION TO MY DEFAULT: I kept optimising for the QUALITY OF MY EXPLANATION when the user was measuring the COMPLETENESS OF THE RECIPIENT'S INPUTS. Those are different targets and only the second one matters in a handoff -- my explanation is not present when the other agent runs. Distinct from the durability pattern (KB 586, 'did the work persist at all'): this one is 'given that it persisted, can the recipient actually act on it without asking anyone'. DIRECTIVE: when handing work to another agent or machine, do not reason about whether they will figure it out. Enumerate what they need, check each item is actually present on their side, and where a gap FAILS SILENTLY convert it into an instrument rather than a sentence -- scripts/bootstrap_jarvis.py --check now reports machine state (venv, deps, vector index, hearth, keepalive, unanswered mail) with the fix inline, because a prose warning about a silent failure is itself easy to miss.
